← Chapter 37 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 39 →

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Medium, about 0.7% of the novel (4,630 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Summary

Catherine’s memories of Cousin Hannah are clouded by opium and by her dream of an immortal love, and Mr. Spitzer, being as one dead, must be prodded to remember anything at all. Catherine thought the lonely cause of suffrage unworthy of Hannah’s adventurous spirit and a waste of time. She would have been happy, she insists, if only Peron had lived, and she explains his neglect as a love too great to express: “This dead love which never was and never would be real was the one undying love.” Hannah had invited her to Egypt to show that a woman could be both beautiful and independent of man, and Catherine imagines the life she might have had, picketing Buckingham Palace, sleeping in silken tents, escaping from moated castles. She remembers Hannah’s sharp, masculine virtues with envy and guilt, wonders whom Hannah had loved, and is sorry that Hannah was not a knight or a Prince Charming come to wake her. Mr. Spitzer observes that most people are disoriented as to time, place, and person, and Vera calls the house what it has become, “this loony bin.”

Chapter 57: The Tailor's Bill

← Chapter 56 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 58 →

Story arc: Arc 5 Mr. Spitzer's Grief

Length: Medium, about 0.7% of the novel (4,418 words)

Character hubs: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Great Tailor

Summary

A polite, threatening bill keeps arriving from Peron’s tailor for the black funeral suit Mr. Spitzer is sure he paid for in cash, without receipts. In a recurring dream he journeys to pay it twice and finds no tailor, only empty lofts, and wakes from seeing himself in Peron’s brown derby. Awake, he searches Boston for the tailor’s shop, turning left for right because dreams go by opposites. At the Public Library he combs city directories and old newspapers and finds Peron’s death notice and his own name in the society columns, but no tailor and no street. Beside him a man argues with a dead man about the soul, and a young man who cannot be older than twenty swears he took a bullet at Appomattox, where the South won. Outside, at twilight, Mr. Spitzer watches the clouds become a skull, a hand, a bird, and a rose, and wishes for a rose named for both brothers, red and white on a single bush.

Summary

The bus reaches the Tavern at the end of its journey and cannot wedge into the space between a leaking milk truck and a hearse. Moses Hunnecker, drunk or so Vera thinks, curses old Doc, the mad Dr. Justice O’Leary, whose invisible ghost buggy, an old Ford full of the children Moses jeers at, he believes is taking the space. Vera, Madge, and Homer stay in their seats out of infinite weariness, for they have come home to no home. Chapter 55: Carpe Diem Hoc Opus, Hic Labor Est

← Chapter 54 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 56 →

Story arc: Arc 5 Mr. Spitzer's Grief

Length: Long, about 1.8% of the novel (12,175 words)

Character hubs: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Summary

Mr. Spitzer imagines the life he would have led if his brother had died first: his theoretical music, his butterflies and postage stamps, safe investments in sunken ships and dead Russian bonds, and a tenth symphony that would begin where other composers had ended their lives. He remembers the twin house he designed so that each brother had his half, every portrait, garden, and mirror repeated, and how Peron mocked it, moved the furniture, forged Joachim’s checks, and never did him a single favor. Since Peron’s death his eyes see double, the near things small and the far things large; he sleeps with his eyes open and wakes in the wrong carriage, the wrong passenger behind a skeleton coachman. Peron lived by carpe diem, Joachim by hoc opus, hic labor est. The walls of the twin house have been knocked down, and Mr. Spitzer, broken by the funeral and its debts, lives in an old beach-comber’s house, “still wondering whose funeral it was.”

Chapter 78: Little Jackass

← Chapter 77 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 79 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes cruelty to a young child and a stillbirth.

Story arc: Arc 8 Esther Longtree

Length: Medium, about 0.7% of the novel (4,933 words)

Character hubs: Esther Longtree · Esther’s Father · Esther’s Mother · Rosemary Longtree

Summary

Esther was called Little Jackass from birth, because she was born kicking and stubborn. She grew up lonely, bullied at school for her deformed foot and crossed eyes, always stung by bees, always falling. Her tiny, cold mother, a pallid descendant of George Washington’s sister, hit her, tied her by a rope to a tree in the yard, and blamed her all her life for the death of her twin, Rosemary, whom Esther had kicked out of the womb months early, stillborn and buried under an unnamed pear tree; Rosemary would have been the perfect daughter. As a child Esther dug for her with a spoon and found only a thimble, beads, a broken doll, the toys of the dead. She loves her father, the passive policeman, who patrols the graveyard whistling to warn off the lovers and whose own mother spilled babies like leaves; she embarrasses her mother by telling that her father has a Negro streak and that her mother’s brother killed himself. She wonders whether she herself is the shadow, the one who never truly lived.

Chapter 39: The Infinite House

← Chapter 38 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 40 →

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Medium, about 0.7% of the novel (4,924 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · The Black Coachman · Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton · Mr. Res Tacamah

Summary

Vera reflects on the irony that Cousin Hannah, a rationalist in the avant-garde of suffrage, became for Catherine a figure of dead romance, a knight errant who could not be held to mortal law. Catherine, lonely and drugged, half believes she imagined Hannah’s visit: “It was as if the perpendicular pronoun I had come to see my horizontal mother.” Her “I” means many things. She is the chair, the lamp, Brooklyn Bridge, a great hostess and a recluse at once, travelling everywhere without leaving the house. Her soul is a house of endless rooms, and in every room someone is missing. She knows that opium has poisoned all pleasures at their source, and that knowledge of so many selves has only added to her torment. Her sanity, she believes, is simply knowing that she is insane, and she would not trade her beautiful false selves for one dull true one. She greets her phantoms, Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton, who twitters like a cage of canaries, and Mr. Res Tacamah, the drug bottle with very large ears, and wonders whether God, too, is dreaming opium dreams, and whether dream and reality are the same.

Chapter 2: The Beautiful Corpse

← Chapter 1 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 3 →

Story arc: Arc 1 The Bus Ride

Length: Very long, about 2.3% of the novel (15,386 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Jock Cartwheel · The Black Coachman · The Canary · The Egyptian Sailor · James the Chauffeur · Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Res Tacamah · The Sea-House Servants · Vera’s Grandparents (Catherine’s Parents)

Summary

Vera describes her mother, Catherine. She is an opium addict who has lain in bed for years among jewels and phantoms and treats her hallucinations as more real than the world. The chapter traces how she came to this. There was a brief marriage to Jock Cartwheel, and a love triangle with twin brothers: Catherine loved Peron Spitzer, who did not love her, while his brother Joachim loved Catherine without return. Joachim, Mr. Spitzer, is the family lawyer and visits her bedside every evening. An Egyptian sailor arrives looking for the dead Peron and mistakes Joachim for him, and Catherine gives the sailor elaborate directions through her labyrinthine house. There is also the chauffeur, James, with whom she once tried to run away. Whenever her canary dies, Mr. Spitzer secretly replaces it. The chapter ends when a canary escapes into a thunderstorm. Catherine calmly accepts that she must now live forever and dismisses its distant twittering as another dream.

Chapter 44: False Modesty Killed My Love

← Chapter 43 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 45 →

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Medium, about 0.7% of the novel (4,441 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Summary

Over the years Mr. Spitzer pieces together the truth of Cousin Hannah’s last days. The great bloomer girl, who spent her life urging ladies to take off their skirts, called for her skirt as she died. When he brought her snowdrops, they melted in her hand, and from that moment she began to fade. In her delirium she relived a climb in the snowbound mountains: her love, “my lovely bride,” turned back to find her skirt, out of a modesty Hannah calls false since there was no one to see, and was lost in the snow. Hannah blamed herself for letting go, and Mr. Spitzer understands at last that this lost love drove her suffrage battles and her wanderings. He wonders whether great heroes are driven by secret cowardice, whether the burning moth is braver than the star, and whether suffrage was only her mask. In her papers he finds letters in languages no one can read, many like love letters to a great love, and he remembers a sea shell he once found, written over: “For all dead loves and all remembered things. I have travelled through many seas.” Perhaps he knows most of love who never loved.

Summary

On a rainy afternoon in the dark restaurant, Esther tells Vera about Walter, her first-born. When she was a young girl, a stranger found her asleep in the summer fields, and she woke with him already inside her; at dawn she saw that he was a Black man, his face scarred where a white mob in the South had tried to hang him because he smiled at a white old maid’s rooster. Yet she believes Walter lives, a Boy Scout raised by kind white people, and he follows her everywhere, asking why she killed him and where his father is. She sets out crumbs for the spirits, knits with invisible thread, and waits for the little shadow boxer to make up for the first.

Summary

Vera describes the heaven Catherine expects, as disordered as this world: drifting mirrors, ceilings that become floors, clocks striking inept hours. Catherine has always said that order is “a mad man’s dream,” and that Mr. Spitzer, “wishing to be agreeable, had made a false report as to what might be upon the other side.” Drugged and nearly inert, she cannot tell life from death, and asks who the dreamer is. She recalls Hannah’s adventures in the harems, unveiling her bearded face to a sheik who went mad, and bowing to a sheik who proved to be a beautiful woman. Summary

In the full light of dawn, Vera studies the sleeping woman. Summary

Reading by candlelight the letters strangers wrote to Cousin Hannah, asking about lost loves, dead brides, and vanished bridegrooms, Mr. Spitzer marvels that one who never loved should have been taken for an authority on love. From her last ravings he pieces together her secret. She had climbed the snowbound mountains with “her acolyte, her beautiful girl,” who went back over the peak to find her skirt and never returned. Hannah believed she had let go the girl’s hand and killed her love, and that guilt drove all her suffrage battles, yet at the end she cries that it was the girl who let go: “We were two lone women. There was no man.” She dies asking forgiveness, a sea shell roaring at her feet, and is buried in a grey New England churchyard. Mr. Spitzer resolves to keep her secret and wonders what image could mark her grave, perhaps a milestone reading “Twelve Miles.” He mourns how quickly the world forgets, thinking of the pigeons of Boston and Venice and the vanished passenger pigeons, and he is no longer sure whether he is Joachim or Peron.

Summary

Esther’s parents, the huge passive policeman and his tiny child-bride, never consummated their marriage. For seven years a large, dark, foreign woman in a man’s hat, coat, and shoes came at night to their kitchen, carrying a tiny silver spoon between husband and wife while the policeman read old baseball scores behind the stove, until Esther and Rosemary were conceived. When the mother went alone to the go-between’s mule farm to show her the pregnancy, the go-between took her into bed and held her down, and in that minute the mother saw that it was a man; afterward she tried and failed to get rid of the child. Esther’s uncle, a pugilist, told her the story, laughing. On her seventh birthday her mother, dressed in her old bridal clothes, led her all day through briers and marshes to the old mule farm, where the go-between lay dying and blind on a bed of chicken feathers, with Esther’s own crooked nose and dimpled chin: her father. Ever since, every day has been her birthday, and she has died with every moth.

Summary

At breakfast the morning after her dream, Vera tries to see Miss MacIntosh as she always has: the Rock of Ages, the plain, red-haired nursemaid of common sense who scolds the tide, hates the Emperor Constantine for changing the calendar, and rails against Benjamin Franklin and the electric lights that have robbed the poor of the dark. But Vera has seen her bald in the night. She strikes the table and demands the truth: Miss MacIntosh wears a wig and has neither eyebrows nor eyelashes. Miss MacIntosh answers in grief and wild humor, by way of Canute and Constantine, Jonas Hanway and the umbrella that made every man his own coachman, and the brothers who called her George, and at last she lifts off her red wig. She is bald, her left breast is gone, and she was broke when she first came, which is why they saved the electric lights. Vera promises always to love her. Miss MacIntosh tells her to eat her breakfast, that people are never quite what they seem, that nobody knows anybody, and that she suffers especially when there are rainbows.

Length: Short, about 0.5% of the novel (3,076 words)

Summary

In the moonlight Miss MacIntosh stands by the window, and Vera sees that she is bald, “bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” with “only one breast.” Vera knows her only by her broken nose. Terrified and wildly triumphant at having always pictured her with a mustache and cast her as the bridegroom, Vera screams, “Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!” A struggle follows, told in the language of the boxing ring. Vera is knocked down, her mouth covered by “his hoary hand,” and laid on the bed, and she wonders whether her attacker is a fallen angel, a gladiator, the sandbag dummy come to life, or the angel Jacob wrestled. She calls it the work of someone “who should take advantage of a poor, ignorant girl, only fourteen years old.” She calls for her mother and for Mr. Spitzer, but no one comes. In the morning her braids are exactly braided, and the only scratches on her cheeks could have come from leafless branches.

Summary

Esther wonders whether her successful conceptions were her worst mistakes. She tells of the Chicago detective, who wears disguises and solves every mystery but his own, above all the “quiet, quiet mysteries” where no bodies are missed; he writes that he will track her to her grave if she does not produce his living children. At a breakfast table laid, for no reason anyone names, with Haviland china, silver, and a bowl of white roses, Vera sits scratched, bruised, and aching, “seethingly irritated” that Miss MacIntosh never asks how she passed the night. In the empty playroom Vera finds, on the little blackboard, a message in red chalk ending, “and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.”

Summary

Esther dreads the trial she expects next autumn, when the town’s women will crowd the courthouse to accuse her and she will be unable to produce the three children the Chicago detective says she killed. Her worst mistake, she thinks, was writing to him, a father who was not dying. Summary

Vera Cartwheel rides a Grey Goose bus through the mist of the American Midwest. The driver, Moses Hunnecker, has long bushy hair. He whistles, drinks openly from a whiskey bottle, calls on God and the angels, and drives erratically. She is searching for Miss MacIntosh, the plain, red-haired nursemaid from What Cheer, Iowa, who disappeared or died. Summary

“That was the false dawn, surely.” Vera wakes in Miss MacIntosh’s bed, sure that the night was a dream for which no one was responsible. Before she opens her eyes, she goes over things she never thought to question: the missing eyebrows, the face that changes color, the baseball cap in the mornings, the green ribbon in the evenings, the veils over the whaler’s hat, the black umbrella carried even indoors. Then Vera observes “what I must surely have always known.” One breast has been amputated, and “what was left was no bigger than a baby’s.”

After death, Catherine still travels, and she insists that only a hair’s breadth lies between life and death. Summary

In a thieves’ café, Mr. Spitzer befriends an old mute who has trained a frog to speak in his mouth. Summary

Summary

In a frozen cosmos where ice covers the rivers, the boats, the archer, and the constellations, Mr. Spitzer lives when he is dead and wakes only when he sleeps. He weeps for others who do not weep for him, and above all for Martha, the last passenger pigeon, whose death he dates to September 14, 1918, “in a war-torn world” (she died September 1, 1914). He arrived too late to see her alive, rode all night on the train that carried her body to Washington, and begged the old caretaker of the Washington Museum to set a mirror before her so that she would not know she was alone; the caretaker refused, saying she had no soul and that it was the incapacity to be deceived which caused extinction. Mr. Spitzer would have indicted America before the Senate for what it had done to the pigeons and to the Indians, but he would have been threatened with the Federal pen. He remembers meeting an old sailor, the sole survivor of a shipwreck, and telling him that the greatest shipwreck is to sink when there is no storm. He comes to trust only the false, the blind, and the deaf, all who have lost, and walking through the rain among the pigeons he cannot tell whether he is one or two, or which brother he is.

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Medium, about 0.8% of the novel (5,632 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Summary

Everything seems off key and out of course to Mr. Spitzer, the universe tacking like the wild white snow bird and every room doubling, so that when he sees two golden chairs in the clouds he does not know which is the dream. He steps lightly, breathes softly, and pauses before every door lest it open on the void, for he believes he is living his life after death and may be the one dreamer who dreams not. It was not from the opium lady, who waits for him as for his dead self, nor from the invalid lady, who mistook life for death, that he learned that all that happened happened only once. Life is a moment’s fading luminosity, and he is not the Holy Writ but the flyleaf stuck between the testaments, ground between the zenith stone and the nadir stone, leaving no water-mark, no signature, no name. His little firefly is his key of gold and perhaps all there is. He walks like the tide, advancing as he retreats. He learned much from the old suffragette captain, for whom the hyphen in her name was more important than the two names it joined; she died before he came, and for her he wrote this nocturne.

Summary

Mr. Spitzer remembers closing the estate of the old suffragette, who reminds him of his own duplicity and duality. From old newspapers he learns that her wildest legends were true: she lost her lady on a mountain peak when the girl went back for a white skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots, challenged a prime minister to a duel, chained herself to a lamp-post, flew over the Alps in a plane with canvas wings until the Swiss drew up claims against her for the League of Nations, fought a golden eagle, and came back from the Holy Lands in black skirts and a turban. Searching her house by lamplight, he finds ten thousand shoe horns, an acorn in an iron safe, telephones that do not work, and forty trunks that open only after long trials with forty keys, with always one key or one lid left over. The trunks hold wedding gowns and veils, and no bride’s slippers. Believing she had wished to be the bride, he leaves the gowns out of his inventory to keep her secret. At dawn he finds she has turned a page of the book she was reading when she died, perhaps Eloise et Abelard, and he closes her eyes with two pennies, one in memory of the sun and one in memory of the moon.

Summary

In silk hat and black cape, Mr. Spitzer keeps watch at Cousin Hannah’s deathbed, unsure whether he himself is living or dead. Hannah’s dying becomes a dance of death. She raves through deserts, mountains, and snow, asks whether the lid of the sky is raising or lowering, and speaks to the Emperor Tiberius, a blacksmith, a golden archer, and the Black Moor she calls her love, asking whether she is the anvil or the hammer. The suffrage captain who scorned feminine frivolity longs now for silk skirts, gold-fringed parasols, and her mirror, and Mr. Spitzer wonders whether she had always been “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask.” She searches for “my nymph, my lovely girl,” “my wild swan girl,” and Mr. Spitzer sees her going down like an old ship that no calker can mend. At the end she cries for “my skirt I lost so long ago” and asks, “should love be extinguished by death?”

Summary

Mr. Spitzer, roused for once from his lethargy, accuses Catherine of never having loved any living being. He lives “at this second remove from reality,” hearing every sound a minute late, a counterfeit of himself who fears that any change of habit would bring the skies down. He is conservative where she is radical, and she has never distinguished imagination from memory. Catherine’s mind is on Cousin Hannah, whom she would woo back from death for a winter’s visit, though Hannah never answers her invitations, which Catherine has probably not yet sent. She blames Mr. Spitzer, the last to see Hannah alive, for refusing to say where Hannah has gone, and suspects he is jealous of a returning spirit. She imagines Hannah’s travels from Moscow to Babylon and across Al Sirat into a Moslem paradise without women, and wonders whether Hannah has become a man or a woman. If a woman should be in heaven, she thinks, it would not be heaven long.

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Medium, about 0.8% of the novel (5,276 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Homer Capehorn · The Black Coachman · Mr. Chandelier

Summary

Catherine remembers her wedding many ways: in white and in black, in a cathedral during a royal funeral, at home with only the black coachman as witness, as an elopement with the robber bridegroom pursued by Cossack horsemen. Most often she was married by a St. Bernard dog who spoke church Latin, gave her the Viaticum, and foretold that her husband would be lost between two frozen peaks. Cousin Hannah told her that marriage was “the death of a woman’s soul” and that no man had ever loved her. Catherine remembers Hannah’s visits: the iron keys jangling at her belt, her wit and metallic energy, her weird dance whenever a cock crowed, her contempt for Joachim. In her company Catherine felt “both very flirtatious and very guilty, trying to resist this man who was no man.” She longs to learn arithmetic and geometry so that she might know whether the great geometer of the universe “was sane or insane.” Hannah always predicted that Joachim would fail Catherine at the crucial moment, as Peron had by his apparent suicide.

Story arc: Arc 6 Miss MacIntosh's Last Month

Length: Very long, about 2.9% of the novel (19,307 words)

Character hubs: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · The Arctic Explorer · John Knox MacIntosh · Lorena · Mercy MacIntosh · Richard MacIntosh

Summary

As August turns to September, Miss MacIntosh, bald and half dressed, plays solitaire and mends a pair of black gloves; Vera reveals that these are the gloves she wore when she walked into the ocean one September morning, leaving her wig, her corset, and her umbrella on the beach. The umbrella was Mr. Bonebreaker’s, and Miss MacIntosh tells the story. Weak after losing her left breast and setting ninepins in a Chicago bowling alley, she was found reeling in the street by Titus Bonebreaker, a vegetarian Gospel salesman from the Ozarks who preached the end of the world through a trumpet and believed his grandmother’s story that he was the true King of Sweden. He called her the little sister who had no breasts, praised the hair she did not have, gave her his watch, and kept postponing their wedding. On the night before it, she stood before him naked and bald under an electric bulb. He fled, leaving his umbrella, and later married a foreign girl to give her child a name. Miss MacIntosh worked among the blind, drifted east, spent her savings in Buffalo on white clothes and an ashen wig, and stood alone among the honeymooners at Niagara Falls.

Chapter 51: The Trumpeter or the Trumpeter's Cry

← Chapter 50 · Chapter Hubs Home · Chapter 52 →

Story arc: Arc 4 Cousin Hannah

Length: Very long, about 2.2% of the novel (14,901 words)

Character hubs: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · The Black Coachman · Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Mouse · The Old Horn-Blower

Summary

Puffing along the shore with his mantle growing around him, Mr. Spitzer cannot tell whether he is the conductor lifting his baton, the lamp-lighter, or the oarsman striking light from the waves of darkness. He is the doctor who has lost his patient, the lawyer who has lost his client, lawyer to a starfish, a dead coachman, and the moon in the cloud, and the old postman knocking at every door. He fears being right more than being wrong, removes the stones from a road and puts one back lest he change rivers in their course, and trusts the past more than the future. He signs illegal documents as if they were legal and stamps wills with the wrong seals, once with the seal of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, while Mr. Mouse gnaws his lawsuits and eats his chords. Respecting other people’s mirages because he is a mirage himself, he meets a lady whose twirling zodiac umbrella moves time, an old woman who thinks she is a bird cage, deaf music critics who hear every error, two pianists who play in perfect time only when a thousand miles apart, and an old woman who believed she was a reindeer and was found with a golden arrow through her breast. He lives by mourning the death of the deathless one, and he concludes that the dream of life, like that of death, must ever contain the unrealized, else all would be complete.

Summary

On the Library steps Mr. Spitzer meets an old violinist with a wounded chin and a wild white mane who plays an imaginary violin, and he recognizes the soundless tune at once: a forgotten waltz by a minor nineteenth-century composer, remembered from his childhood. Watching, he decides that the player might have been anyone with a different stick in his hand, batter, billiard player, shepherd, judge, fisherman, king, or conductor, for reality is made of just so many sticks. The music turns his thoughts to Peron, to the broken old sportsmen Peron befriended, and to Peron’s fatal leap. He fears the old man is having a fit or is already dead, but is afraid to applaud or offer money. He has come to distinguish less and less between reality and his dreams, and suspects that this may be his only wisdom.

Summary

Vera thinks of all she could have confessed to Esther. Her mother is dead. The sea swept away the house with its golden towers, leaving chandeliers strewn along the shore, and only the string of pearls she wears remains to her. She is mourning three deaths. At the end, Catherine rose from her bed and walked. Mr. Spitzer carried her into the garden by the sea and declared his love. He told her he was really Peron, and that it was Joachim who had died. Whatever is hidden is the revealed." At dawn in the hotel corridor she meets a stone deaf man, who lost his hearing at fourteen. They become lovers, and he whispers that their child will be his ear. They plan to marry and invite everyone, the flowers and birds and Esther Longtree, who hangs a misspelled sign in the restaurant window, "Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale."
